question: According to the manual, is stopping always the safest response when an emergency arises on the road?
choice_a: No -- when there isn't enough room to stop, steering away from the hazard may be safer
choice_b: Yes, coming to a complete stop is always the safest option
choice_c: Only if you are driving a bus
choice_d: Only when traveling under 30 mph
explanation: The manual states stopping is not always the safest thing to do in an emergency; when you don't have enough room to stop, you may have to steer away from what's ahead.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why does the manual recommend keeping both hands on the steering wheel at all times while driving?
choice_a: It reduces engine wear
choice_b: It gives you the firm grip needed to turn quickly if an emergency requires an evasive steering maneuver
choice_c: It is required for cruise control to engage
choice_d: It prevents the steering wheel from locking
explanation: The best way to have both hands on the wheel in an emergency is to keep them there all the time, so you have a firm grip to turn quickly.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What can happen if you apply the brake while making an emergency steering maneuver to avoid an obstacle?
choice_a: The transmission automatically downshifts
choice_b: The vehicle's cruise control disengages
choice_c: The wheels can lock up, causing you to skid out of control
choice_d: The parking brake engages automatically
explanation: The manual warns not to apply the brake while turning because it's very easy to lock your wheels, and if that happens you may skid out of control.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: If an oncoming driver has drifted into your lane, which direction does the manual say is generally best to steer?
choice_a: Left, into the oncoming driver's lane
choice_b: Straight ahead while braking hard
choice_c: Onto the centerline
choice_d: To your right
explanation: If an oncoming driver has drifted into your lane, a move to your right is best; if the driver realizes what has happened, the natural response is to return to their own lane.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Which braking method involves applying the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, using only small steering adjustments?
choice_a: Controlled braking
choice_b: Stab braking
choice_c: Engine braking
choice_d: Emergency parking-brake braking
explanation: With controlled braking, you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements very small.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: Why does the manual warn against simply jamming down on the brake pedal as hard as possible in an emergency?
choice_a: It can damage the transmission
choice_b: It keeps the wheels locked up, causing a skid and loss of control
choice_c: It automatically triggers the hazard lights
choice_d: It drains the vehicle's battery
explanation: Emergency braking does not mean pushing the pedal as hard as you can; that only keeps the wheels locked up and causes a skid, and if the wheels are skidding you cannot control the vehicle.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What are the two main reasons most hydraulic brake failures occur, according to the manual?
choice_a: Worn tires and a dead battery
choice_b: Faulty turn signals and low fuel
choice_c: Loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills
choice_d: Overinflated tires and a cracked windshield
explanation: The manual states most hydraulic brake failures occur for one of two reasons: loss of hydraulic pressure, or brake fade on long hills.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: If you must use the parking/emergency brake to slow the vehicle after a hydraulic brake failure, what should you do at the same time?
choice_a: Shift into reverse
choice_b: Turn off the engine
choice_c: Turn on the headlights
choice_d: Press the release button or pull the release lever to adjust brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking up
explanation: The manual instructs that when using the emergency brake, you should press the release button or pull the release lever at the same time so you can adjust brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking up.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: On a long downgrade, once the brakes have failed, what does the manual say is usually a driver's best hope for stopping safely?
choice_a: An escape ramp
choice_b: Shifting into neutral and coasting to a stop
choice_c: Sounding the horn continuously to clear traffic
choice_d: Turning off the engine while still moving
explanation: The manual says your best hope is an escape ramp, and that every year hundreds of drivers avoid injury or damage by using them.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: What is a major sign that one of the front tires has failed, according to the manual?
choice_a: The engine temperature gauge spikes
choice_b: The steering feels "heavy"
choice_c: The fuel gauge drops sharply
choice_d: The radio cuts out
explanation: The manual lists "feel" as a sign of tire failure: if the steering feels heavy, it is probably a sign that one of the front tires has failed.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: Immediately after a tire fails, what does the manual say you should do regarding the brakes?
choice_a: Brake hard immediately no matter what
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly at highway speed
choice_c: Stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed, then brake gently, pull off the road, and stop
choice_d: Apply only the parking brake at full speed
explanation: Braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control, so unless you're about to run into something, you should stay off the brake until slowed, then brake gently and pull off the road.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: What does the manual say about ABS and a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: ABS increases stopping power on dry pavement
choice_b: ABS replaces the need for brake pads
choice_c: ABS doubles maximum brake line pressure
choice_d: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes and does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to your normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: When does the Antilock Braking System (ABS) activate?
choice_a: Only when the wheels are about to lock up
choice_b: Continuously, at every brake application
choice_c: Only when driving above 55 mph
choice_d: Only when the parking brake is set
explanation: The manual states ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18 Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What component decreases brake pressure to avoid wheel lockup once sensors detect it is about to occur?
choice_a: The speed retarder
choice_b: The electronic control unit (ECU)
choice_c: The parking brake lever
choice_d: The turbocharger
explanation: Sensors detect potential wheel lockup, and an electronic control unit (ECU) then decreases brake pressure to avoid it.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.1 How Antilock Braking Systems Work

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after which date are required to have ABS, per the manual?
choice_a: March 1, 1995
choice_b: March 1, 1999
choice_c: March 1, 1997
choice_d: March 1, 2001
explanation: The manual states the Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.2 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lbs or more are required to have ABS if built on or after which date?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 2000
choice_d: March 1, 1999
explanation: The manual lists hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999 as requiring ABS.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.2 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: How can you tell that a tractor, truck, or bus is equipped with ABS?
choice_a: It has a yellow ABS malfunction lamp on the instrument panel
choice_b: It has a green indicator light that stays on at all times
choice_c: The horn sounds twice at startup
choice_d: There is no way to tell without disassembling the brakes
explanation: Tractors, trucks, and buses will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the instrument panel.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: The manual describes one exception that allows a driver to fully apply the brakes during an emergency stop with ABS. What is it?
choice_a: When driving downhill only
choice_b: When driving a straight truck or combination vehicle with working ABS on all axles
choice_c: When the trailer is empty
choice_d: When the ABS malfunction lamp is illuminated
explanation: The manual states there is only one exception: if you drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, in an emergency stop you can fully apply the brakes.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.6 Braking with ABS

question: Which of the following is true about ABS, according to the manual's safety reminders?
choice_a: ABS allows you to safely follow other vehicles more closely
choice_b: ABS will always shorten your stopping distance
choice_c: ABS won't prevent skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
choice_d: ABS eliminates the need for regular brake maintenance
explanation: The manual states ABS won't prevent power or turning skids -- it should prevent brake-induced skids or jackknifes, but not those caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: How does the manual describe ABS in relation to your vehicle's normal brakes?
choice_a: As a full replacement for the normal braking system
choice_b: As a system that only functions on dry pavement
choice_c: As a substitute for safe driving habits
choice_d: As an "add-on" to your normal brakes that does not increase or decrease ultimate stopping power
explanation: The manual states ABS won't increase or decrease ultimate stopping power because it is an add-on to your normal brakes, not a replacement for them.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: Which of the following is NOT listed by the manual as one of the four causes of skids?
choice_a: An under-inflated spare tire in the storage compartment
choice_b: Over-braking
choice_c: Over-steering
choice_d: Over-acceleration
explanation: The manual lists four causes of skids: over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast; an under-inflated spare tire is not one of them.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What is the most common type of skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: A front-wheel skid
choice_b: A drive-wheel skid, in which the rear wheels lose traction
choice_c: A trailer-only skid unrelated to the tractor
choice_d: A steering-axle skid caused by low tire pressure
explanation: The manual states the most common skid is one in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: If your drive wheels begin to spin from over-acceleration on ice or snow, what is an easy way to stop the skid?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake hard
choice_b: Turn the steering wheel sharply in either direction
choice_c: Take your foot off the accelerator
choice_d: Downshift into a higher gear
explanation: Skids caused by acceleration usually happen on ice or snow, and taking your foot off the accelerator can easily stop them.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: In a vehicle towing a trailer, what can a rear-wheel braking skid (drive-wheel skid) lead to?
choice_a: The front tires losing air pressure
choice_b: The ABS system permanently disabling
choice_c: The engine stalling immediately
choice_d: The trailer pushing the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife
explanation: With vehicles towing trailers, a drive-wheel skid can let the trailer push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: To correct a drive-wheel braking skid, what does the manual say you should do first?
choice_a: Stop braking, to let the rear wheels roll again
choice_b: Apply the parking brake fully
choice_c: Turn off the engine
choice_d: Accelerate hard to regain traction
explanation: The manual instructs that to correct a drive-wheel braking skid you should first stop braking, which lets the rear wheels roll again and keeps them from sliding.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.2 Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: Which of the following are common causes of a front-wheel skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: A malfunctioning ABS lamp only
choice_b: Driving too fast for conditions, lack of tread on the front tires, and cargo loaded so not enough weight is on the front axle
choice_c: Using the parking brake while parked
choice_d: Overinflated rear tires
explanation: The manual states driving too fast for conditions causes most front-wheel skids, with other causes including lack of tread on the front tires and cargo loaded so not enough weight is on the front axle.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: In a front-wheel skid, how does the front end of the vehicle typically behave?
choice_a: It swings rapidly from side to side
choice_b: It corrects itself automatically without driver input
choice_c: It tends to go in a straight line regardless of how much you turn the steering wheel
choice_d: It lifts off the road surface
explanation: In a front-wheel skid, the front end tends to go in a straight line regardless of how much you turn the steering wheel.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident scene, according to the manual?
choice_a: Call your employer, take photos, exchange insurance information
choice_b: Move all vehicles immediately, call a tow truck, leave the scene
choice_c: Turn off your flashers, block oncoming traffic, wait for police
choice_d: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
explanation: The manual states the basic steps to be taken at any accident are to protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20 Accident Procedures

question: If you were not involved in an accident but stop to help, where should you park?
choice_a: Away from the accident, since the area immediately around it will be needed for emergency vehicles
choice_b: Directly beside the wrecked vehicles
choice_c: In the opposing lane of traffic
choice_d: Blocking the accident vehicles' path
explanation: The manual advises that if you're stopping to help, you should park away from the accident because the area immediately around it will be needed for emergency vehicles.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.1 Protect the Area

question: If you have a cell phone or CB radio at an accident scene, when does the manual say you should call for assistance?
choice_a: Only after moving all vehicles off the road
choice_b: Before you get out of your vehicle
choice_c: Only if someone else at the scene asks you to
choice_d: After waiting at least 15 minutes to assess the situation
explanation: The manual instructs that if you have a cell phone or CB, call for assistance before you get out of your vehicle.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.2 Notify Authorities

question: What does the manual advise about moving a severely injured person after an accident?
choice_a: Move them immediately to a more comfortable position
choice_b: Move them only if a bystander suggests it
choice_c: Don't move them unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary
choice_d: Move them away from the vehicle regardless of injury type
explanation: The manual states not to move a severely injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: How does the manual say you should stop heavy bleeding when assisting an injured person?
choice_a: By elevating the vehicle
choice_b: By having the person walk around
choice_c: By applying ice directly to the open wound
choice_d: By applying direct pressure to the wound
explanation: The manual instructs to stop heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: Which of the following is listed as a cause of tire-related vehicle fires?
choice_a: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
choice_b: An overfilled fuel tank
choice_c: A cracked windshield
choice_d: Worn seat belts
explanation: The manual lists under-inflated tires and duals that touch as causes of tire fires.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: What is the first step the manual recommends if your vehicle catches fire while driving?
choice_a: Open all doors and windows immediately
choice_b: Pull off the road and park in an open area away from buildings, trees, brush, and other vehicles
choice_c: Remove all cargo before doing anything else
choice_d: Call your dispatcher and wait for further instructions before stopping
explanation: The first step in the manual's fire procedures is to pull off the road and stop, parking in an open area away from buildings, trees, brush, other vehicles, or anything that might catch fire.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: For a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, what does the manual advise about the doors, especially if the cargo includes hazardous materials?
choice_a: Open them immediately to ventilate the smoke
choice_b: Remove them completely to access the fire
choice_c: Keep them shut, since opening them supplies the fire with oxygen and can make it burn faster
choice_d: It does not matter whether the doors are open or shut
explanation: The manual says to keep the doors shut for a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, especially with hazardous materials, because opening them will supply oxygen and can cause it to burn very fast.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: When using a fire extinguisher, where should you aim it?
choice_a: Up into the flames
choice_b: At the top of the vehicle
choice_c: Anywhere near visible smoke
choice_d: At the source or base of the fire
explanation: The manual instructs to aim at the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: Which type of fire extinguisher is designed to work on burning wood, paper, and cloth in addition to electrical fires and burning liquids?
choice_a: The A:B:C type
choice_b: The B:C type only
choice_c: A water-only extinguisher
choice_d: A purple K dry chemical extinguisher only
explanation: The manual states the A:B:C type is designed to work on burning wood, paper, and cloth as well as electrical fires and burning liquids, which the B:C type alone handles.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: Why does the manual warn against using water on an electrical fire?
choice_a: It evaporates too quickly to be effective
choice_b: It can cause an electric shock
choice_c: It is too heavy for most extinguisher tanks
choice_d: It permanently damages fire extinguisher equipment
explanation: The manual states water can be used on wood, paper, or cloth, but not on an electrical fire because it can cause shock.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: According to the manual's fire class chart, Class D fires (combustible metals) should be extinguished using:
choice_a: Water only
choice_b: Foam
choice_c: Specialized extinguishing powders
choice_d: Carbon dioxide only
explanation: The manual's fire class chart shows Class D fires in combustible metals are extinguished by using specialized extinguishing powders.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: According to the manual, how does alcohol affect a driver?
choice_a: It only affects reaction time, with no impact on judgment
choice_b: It has no measurable effect below a BAC of .08
choice_c: It affects only night vision, not coordination
choice_d: It impairs muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception, and night vision, and affects judgment and inhibition
explanation: The manual states alcohol impairs muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception, and night vision, and also affects the parts of the brain that control judgment and inhibition.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: At what rate does the manual say the liver can process alcohol?
choice_a: About one-third of an ounce per hour, a fixed rate
choice_b: About two ounces per hour
choice_c: As fast as it enters the bloodstream
choice_d: About one ounce per hour, increasing with body weight
explanation: The manual states the liver can only process one-third of an ounce of alcohol per hour, which is a fixed rate.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What does the manual say will actually sober up a person who has been drinking?
choice_a: Black coffee
choice_b: Only time, since the liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate
choice_c: A cold shower
choice_d: Physical exercise
explanation: Because the liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate, only time -- not black coffee or a cold shower -- will sober you up.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: Which set of drinks does the manual identify as containing the same amount of alcohol?
choice_a: Two beers and one glass of wine
choice_b: A 12-oz beer and a 12-oz glass of wine
choice_c: A 12-oz glass of 5% beer, a 5-oz glass of 12% wine, and a 1.5-oz shot of 80 proof liquor
choice_d: Two shots of liquor and one beer
explanation: The manual states a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of 80 proof liquor all contain the same amount of alcohol.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What three factors determine Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC), according to the manual?
choice_a: Time of day, vehicle type, and road conditions
choice_b: Age, gender, and driving experience
choice_c: Fuel type, tire pressure, and vehicle speed
choice_d: The amount of alcohol consumed, how fast you drink it, and your body weight
explanation: The manual states BAC is determined by the amount of alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, and your body weight.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: According to the manual's BAC effects chart, at approximately what BAC level is there "definite impairment in coordination and judgment" marking the drunk driving limit?
explanation: The manual's BAC effects chart lists .08 as showing definite impairment in coordination and judgment, marking the drunk driving limit.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: When is possession and use of a drug prescribed by a doctor permitted while driving, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only if it is an over-the-counter medication
choice_b: If the doctor informs the driver that it will not affect safe driving ability
choice_c: Only if taken once per week or less
choice_d: Only if the driver feels fine after taking it
explanation: The manual states possession and use of a drug given to a driver by a doctor is permitted if the doctor informs the driver it will not affect safe driving ability.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: What does the manual say is the only cure for fatigue?
choice_a: Caffeine
choice_b: Fresh air
choice_c: Rest
choice_d: Cold water splashed on the face
explanation: The manual states you should never use any drug that hides fatigue, because the only cure for fatigue is rest.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: According to the manual, what should you do if you become too ill to operate a motor vehicle safely?
choice_a: Continue driving carefully at a reduced speed
choice_b: Pull over and wait exactly one hour before continuing
choice_c: Call a friend to take over driving your commercial vehicle
choice_d: You must not drive, except in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place you can safely stop
explanation: The manual states if you become too ill to operate a motor vehicle safely, you must not drive, though in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place you can safely stop.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.3 Illness

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: What must all commercial drivers be able to do regarding hazardous cargo, even without a hazardous materials endorsement?
choice_a: Recognize hazardous cargo and know whether they can legally haul it without a hazardous materials endorsement
choice_b: Repackage hazardous materials themselves before transport
choice_c: Determine hazard classes without ever consulting shipping papers
choice_d: Ignore hazardous cargo rules when driving short distances
explanation: The manual states all drivers should know something about hazardous materials, and must be able to recognize hazardous cargo and know whether they can haul it without a hazardous materials endorsement.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23 Hazardous Materials Rules For All Commercial Drivers

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: What two things does a shipper use to communicate the risk of hazardous materials to dockworkers and drivers?
choice_a: A phone call and a follow-up email
choice_b: A shipping paper and diamond-shaped hazard labels
choice_c: A verbal warning and a hand signal
choice_d: A GPS alert and a text message
explanation: The manual states the shipper uses a shipping paper and diamond shaped hazard labels to warn dockworkers and drivers of the risk.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: Where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers while driving, according to the manual?
choice_a: In the glovebox, regardless of accessibility
choice_b: In the sleeper berth
choice_c: In a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle
choice_d: Anywhere in the cab, since location does not matter
explanation: The manual requires shipping papers to be kept in a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: How many identical placards must a placarded vehicle display, and in what positions?
choice_a: Two, on the front and rear only
choice_b: One on each wheel
choice_c: Six, one on each side panel
choice_d: At least four, placed on the front, rear, and both sides
explanation: The manual states a placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, put on the front, rear, and both sides.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: A hazardous materials identification number is a four-digit code preceded by which letters?
choice_a: "NA" or "UN"
choice_b: "HZ" or "DG"
choice_c: "US" or "CA"
choice_d: "EX" or "PL"
explanation: The manual states the identification number will be preceded by the letters "NA" or "UN."
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: What resource lists hazardous chemicals along with their identification numbers, for use by first responders?
choice_a: The vehicle owner's manual
choice_b: The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
choice_c: The state DMV handbook
choice_d: The shipper's sales invoice
explanation: The manual states the US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) lists the chemicals and the identification numbers assigned to them.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: Can a driver operate a vehicle carrying hazardous materials that does not require placards, without holding a hazardous materials endorsement?
choice_a: No, an endorsement is always required for any hazmat cargo
choice_b: Only if the load weighs under 100 pounds
choice_c: Yes, a driver can operate it if the load does not require placards
choice_d: Only with written permission from the shipper
explanation: The manual states you can drive a vehicle that carries hazardous materials if it does not require placards; if it requires placards, you cannot drive it without the hazardous materials endorsement.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: What is required to legally drive a vehicle that requires hazardous materials placards?
choice_a: A valid regular (non-commercial) driver's license
choice_b: A note from the shipping company
choice_c: At least five years of driving experience
choice_d: A commercial driver license with the hazardous materials endorsement
explanation: The manual states the rules require all drivers of placarded vehicles to have a commercial driver license with the hazardous materials endorsement.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

topic: Hazardous Materials Rules for All Drivers
question: A tank endorsement is required for a commercial vehicle designed to transport liquid or gaseous materials in a tank with an individual rated capacity of more than how many gallons (and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more)?
choice_a: 119 gallons
choice_b: 50 gallons
choice_c: 500 gallons
choice_d: 1,000 gallons
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required for any commercial vehicle designed to transport liquid or gaseous materials in a tank with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.
source_note: Oregon Commercial Driver License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products
